doc.title: Ingrid Sertso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, August 11, 2014

title: Hound Dog request in a French club; rock and roll and the blues
summary: In a French club with a German jazz group a rich fan requested Hound Dog; then talk of Big Mama Thornton, rock and jazz mixing, and not being a blues singer.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Well you can not do anything else. You can only do what comes out of your need, what comes out of your personal expression. You cannot do anything else. I was often thinking that I should write a rock & roll song. You know, so we’d make a little bit of more money or something. Forget it. You have to be like that. In Europe I worked in so many clubs before I met Karl. And I worked in a very famous French club with a German jazz group. We went to a lot of jazz festivals. And there was a guy that came every day because he loved the band, and he always sent up some Schnapps, some liquor, and always had some requests. That day I remember another piece of paper came up with a peppermint Schnapps and it said, “Sugar, could you please sing ‘You Ain’t Nothing But a Hound Dog’?” My saxophone player says, “What does it say?” I told him and he said, “Okay let’s rehearse.” I said, “Oh no. I cannot sing that song. I cannot. It’s an Elvis Presley song, it’s an old Gospel, but I can’t sing it, I don’t even know the lyrics.” And the saxophone player, who was the leader, said, “You have to sing it, we get a lot of money from him.” He was a very rich guy, must have been a millionaire. I gave in, we rehearsed in the intermission, and I sang “You Ain’t Nothing But a Hound Dog.” Another piece of paper came up with another peppermint Schnapps, and it said, “Sugar, you will never have to do it again.” I couldn’t do it. He wanted to hear it the way he is used to. I can’t do that. “Thank you Sugar but you never have to do it —”
I suppose you should have been happy that you didn’t do a good job with it because he would have come back and asked you again.

But what I love here is that rock & roll and jazz sometimes, I love that. You know because there’s very good rock & roll musicians, can be. And a lot of musicians we work with also work in the rock & roll thing. So I love that. That’s totally separated in Europe. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
Because the art education is so strict there that the idea of something more commercial weaving into a strict art form, it wouldn’t work. No.
Have you ever heard Big Mama Thornton’s version?
I mean that’s — it’s much more authentic than Elvis, by a long shot. I mean she was a blues shouter.
She’s the one that sang “You Ain’t Nothing But a Hound Dog?”
Yes. And then Elvis covered it. You know. Plus it was written by two young white men, so that the way this music finds its way in and out to these people is very interesting.
Yeah. I’m sure she sang it great. Because it’s a cool song. It’s just that I have no relation to it.
Well is the blues part of your exposure in Germany or France?

No. Not at all. It needed a long time until I sang the blues. I was classically raised you know. But now I was just at a birthday party and there was a singer there and we sang over “Monk Blues” and we scatted like crazy. But I would not go into a lot of blues singing because that’s not really my background and other people can do it much better.
